nysgerrig.explanation: "Nysgerrig" means "curious", as in wanting to know things. To say what you are curious to do, add "efter at" (to): "Han er nysgerrig efter at lære mere" (He is curious to learn more). A second meaning is "nosy", as in asking too much about other people: "Vær ikke så nysgerrig!" (Do not be so nosy!)

nysgerrighed.explanation: "En nysgerrighed" means "curiosity". It comes from "nysgerrig" (curious) with "-hed" added, like "-ness" in English. The same ending turns "fri" (free) into "en frihed" (a freedom).

nytte.explanation: "En nytte" means "a use". To say something helps, use "at gøre nytte" (literally, "to do use"): "Paraplyen gjorde nytte" (The umbrella was useful). To say something is of no use, use "ingen" (no): "Det har ingen nytte" (It is of no use).

nyttig.explanation: "Nyttig" means "useful". It comes from "nytte" (use). To say a piece of advice helps, say: "Det er et nyttigt tip" (That is a useful tip).

nytårsaften.explanation: "Nytårsaften" means "New Year's Eve". It is built from "nytår" (new year) and "aften" (evening). On that evening the Danish monarch gives a speech on television, "nytårstalen" (the New Year's speech).

nå.explanation: "Nå" means "oh". When you have just understood something, say: "Nå, det vidste jeg ikke!" (Oh, I did not know that!) To start a chat again, it also means "well": "Nå, hvad så?" (Well, what's up?)

nå ja.explanation: "Nå ja" means "oh right". When you suddenly remember something, say it first: "Nå ja, nu husker jeg det" (Oh right, now I remember). The small word "jo" (as you know) can follow: "Nå ja, det er jo tirsdag i dag" (Oh right, it is Tuesday today, you know).

nå men.explanation: "Nå men" means "well then". To move a conversation on, say: "Nå men, lad os komme i gang" (Well then, let us get started). To end a conversation, say: "Nå men, jeg må videre" (Well then, I have to move on).

nåde.explanation: "En nåde" means "a mercy". To say a person is merciful, use "at vise nåde" (to show mercy): "Dommeren viste nåde" (The judge showed mercy). A second meaning is "grace": "af Guds nåde" (by the grace of God).

når.explanation: "Når" means "when". For something that happens again and again or has not happened yet, use it like this: "Når det regner, bliver jeg hjemme" (When it rains, I stay home). For one time in the past, use "da" (when): "Da jeg kom hjem, var det mørkt" (When I came home, it was dark). To ask a question, use "hvornår" (when): "Hvornår kommer du?" (When are you coming?)

når som helst.explanation: "Når som helst" means "anytime". To invite someone, say: "Kom når som helst" (Come anytime). To say something might happen without warning, it also means "at any moment": "Det kan regne når som helst" (It can rain at any moment).

næppe.explanation: "Næppe" means "unlikely". To say something will probably not happen, put it after the verb: "Han kommer næppe" (He is unlikely to come). It also means "hardly": "Jeg kan næppe kende ham" (I can hardly recognize him). A tiny chance is left, unlike "aldrig" (never): "Han kommer aldrig" (He never comes).

nær.explanation: "Nær" means "close". To talk about a person you are close to, put it before the noun: "en nær ven" (a close friend). To say a place is close to something, use "tæt på" (close to): "Jeg bor tæt på stationen" (I live close to the station).

nærig.explanation: "Nærig" means "stingy". It is not a compliment. Do not mix it up with "sparsommelig", which means "thrifty": "Hun er sparsommelig og køber brugt" (She is thrifty and buys second-hand).

næringsrig.explanation: "Næringsrig" means "nutritious". It is built from "en næring" (nourishment) and "rig" (rich). To say a meal is nutritious, say: "Det er et næringsrigt måltid" (It is a nutritious meal).

nærmest.explanation: "Nærmest" means "almost". To say you have nearly finished, say: "Jeg er nærmest færdig" (I am almost done). A second meaning is "nearest": "den nærmeste station" (the nearest station).

nærværende.explanation: "Nærværende" means "attentive". To say a father gives you his full attention, say: "Han er en nærværende far" (He is an attentive father). In a formal contract, "nærværende kontrakt" means "this contract".

næseblod.explanation: "Næseblod" means "a nosebleed". It is built from "næse" (nose) and "blod" (blood). To say you have a nosebleed, leave out the article: "Jeg har næseblod" (I have a nosebleed).

næsten.explanation: "Næsten" means "almost". To say you have nearly finished, say: "Jeg er næsten færdig" (I am almost done). Do not mix it up with "næste", which means "next": "næste uge" (next week).

næsten aldrig.explanation: "Næsten aldrig" means "almost never". It is built from "næsten" (almost) and "aldrig" (never). Because "aldrig" already makes the sentence negative, do not add "ikke" (not). To say you rarely do something, say: "Hun spiser næsten aldrig kød" (She almost never eats meat).

nødder.explanation: "Nødder" means "nuts". To name one kind of nut, join its name to "nød": "en hasselnød" (a hazelnut) and "en valnød" (a walnut).

nødhjælp.explanation: "Nødhjælp" means "emergency aid". It is built from "nød" (distress) and "hjælp" (help). To say you collect money for victims of a disaster, say: "Vi samler nødhjælp ind til ofrene" (We collect emergency aid for the victims).

nødig.explanation: "Nødig" means "rather not". Put it after "vil" (will, want) or "ville" (would): "Jeg vil nødig tage afsted" (I would rather not leave). To say someone else would rather not, say: "Hun ville nødig sige det" (She would rather not say it).

nødt til.explanation: "Nødt til" means "have to". When you have no choice, say "er nødt til at" before the verb: "Jeg er nødt til at gå" (I have to go). When you choose to go, say "Jeg vil gå" (I want to go) instead.

nødvendig.explanation: "Nødvendig" means "necessary". To say you cannot do without something, say: "Et pas er nødvendigt" (A passport is necessary). Do not mix it up with "vigtig", which means "important": "Sundhed er vigtig" (Health is important).
